title: Implement profile pack schema + validation (JSON/YAML) with compatibility checks and safe default constraints
creator: Noah Patel
project: Hardware tuning profiles pack (Serving Runtime Performance — Kernel + Scheduling)
description:
Goal
Implement the v1 schema for the “hardware tuning profiles pack” and enforce validation across both JSON and YAML inputs. This includes:
- deterministic validation (no implicit coercions)
- hardware/software compatibility gates (GPU SKU, driver, CUDA)
- safe-default guardrails (memory headroom, concurrency/batching caps, allocator/KV cache constraints)

Context
Profiles are intended to be versioned artifacts that can be shipped with runtime releases and optionally pinned/overridden by Dedicated/Private customers. We need strict validation to avoid silent misconfigurations and to make selection logic safe.

Scope
1) Schema definition (v1)
- Top-level metadata
  - pack_id (string), pack_version (semver-ish string), generated_at (RFC3339 string optional)
  - default_profile_id_by_sku: mapping for H100/L40S/B200 (note: keep matching logic in selection layer; schema just captures defaults)
- Profiles list
  - profile_id (string, unique)
  - sku_match (enum): H100 | L40S | B200
  - compatibility
    - min_driver_version / max_driver_version (semver-ish; allow open ended)
    - min_cuda_version / max_cuda_version
    - mig_mode: allowed values: any | mig | no-mig
    - form_factor: any | pcie | sxm (needed for H100 variance)
  - workload_buckets
    - definitions are validated only (names + numeric bounds), not “correctness” (owned by scheduler work)
  - runtime_knobs
    - scheduler knobs: queue limits, prefill/decode prioritization, batching heuristic id, backpressure thresholds
    - kernel knobs: attention kernel variant id + fallback policy
    - memory/KV cache knobs: target headroom, compaction thresholds, max KV allocation fraction
  - host_tuning (best-effort)
    - cpu_pinning, numa_policy, hugepages, cuda_env (string key/value list). Validation ensures allowed keys only.

2) Parser + loader
- Accept JSON and YAML as inputs (same schema). YAML is a convenience format; runtime normalizes to a single internal representation.
- Provide stable error messages (human-readable) with paths (e.g., profiles[2].compatibility.min_cuda_version).
- Reject unknown fields by default (to prevent config drift). If we need forward-compat, add an explicit “allow_unknown_fields: true” gate later.

3) Compatibility gates (validation time)
- Validate that a profile’s compatibility section is internally consistent:
  - min_* <= max_* when both are provided
  - required fields present for B200 profiles (to avoid accidentally applying H100 defaults)
- Validate that defaults are safe for the target SKU:
  - enforce a min memory headroom floor (e.g., >= 10%) and a max KV cache fraction cap per SKU
  - enforce concurrency/batching caps to prevent known OOM/fragmentation failure modes (L40S is the primary risk)
- Provide a “compatibility matrix” helper that can be used by selection logic to answer “does profile X apply to detected hardware?”. (Selection itself is ENG-4923.)

4) Guardrails for overrides
- Schema must support a notion of which knobs are overrideable later, but the enforcement belongs in the runtime override layer.
- In this ticket: mark fields that are unsafe to override without an explicit ‘unsafe_allow’ flag (e.g., headroom, max_concurrency, allocator aggressive mode). This can be represented as validation rules + a reserved override policy list.

5) Tests and CI hooks
- Unit tests for:
  - round-trip parsing JSON/YAML
  - rejection of unknown fields
  - boundary checks for numeric knobs
  - compatibility gate logic (driver/CUDA min/max)
  - uniqueness (profile_id, sku default mapping)
- Include “bad config fixtures” that assert error messages are actionable.

Non-goals
- Implementing selection precedence (ENG-4923)
- Shipping final tuned knobs for each SKU (separate profile definition tickets)
- Building a full UI/Console surface for editing profiles

Proposed implementation notes
- Runtime repo module: runtime/profilepack (or equivalent)
- Validation approach: typed structs + explicit validation (preferred) OR JSONSchema with strict mode.
- Version parsing: we only need stable comparisons for driver/CUDA ranges; avoid overly fancy semver rules. Driver version comparison should treat components numerically.

Acceptance criteria
- Runtime can load a profile pack from JSON or YAML and produce deterministic validation errors.
- Invalid profiles never silently fall back to defaults; they fail fast (except where selection logic chooses another compatible profile).
- Compatibility rules enforce that B200 profiles require explicit driver/CUDA constraints.
- Safe default constraints prevent known dangerous settings (e.g., L40S headroom too low, unlimited concurrency).
- Tests added and passing in CI.

Links
- Epic: ENG-4921
- Related PR (WIP): https://github.com/redwood/redwood/pull/24873 (loader + initial definitions behind flag)
- Infra constraints doc (reference): sources/confluence/eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity/hardware-sku-constraints-for-profiles.json

Owners / reviewers

- Reviewers: Anika Gupta (conformance/tests), Omar El-Sayed (KV cache guardrails), Irene Choi (fleet compatibility expectations)
comments: 2026-01-14 (Quentin Harris): Drafted v1 schema fields (top-level metadata + profiles[]). Main open question: do we encode workload buckets in the profile pack vs keep them entirely in scheduler config? Proposal: keep bucket names + bounds here for observability tagging, but treat them as validation-only (scheduler decides behavior).

2026-01-18 (Irene Choi): Please include explicit handling for PCIe vs SXM for H100. We’ve seen different perf/stability characteristics with some defaults (esp. memory headroom). Even if we don’t branch yet, add the field so we can gate/select in the future.

2026-01-22 (Omar El-Sayed): Guardrails request: cap kv_cache.max_fraction on L40S aggressively and enforce min headroom >= 15% for the initial pack. We’ve had fragmentation spikes during bursts; better to be conservative and allow opt-in overrides later with audit logs.

2026-01-27 (Anika Gupta): +1 on rejecting unknown fields. Also request: error messages must include JSONPath-ish location and the invalid value. We should add negative fixtures to lock error text format (or at least structure) so on-call can grep logs reliably.

2026-02-03 (Quentin Harris): Implemented YAML parser normalization + strict unknown-field rejection locally. Next up: driver/CUDA range comparison helpers. I’m using numeric tuple comparison; treating missing patch as 0. Will document in module README.

2026-02-06 (Quentin Harris): Open issue: how to compare NVIDIA driver versions reliably across formats (e.g., 550.54.14 vs 550.54). Current plan: parse as up to 3 numeric components; ignore suffixes. If we encounter suffixes in fleet metadata, we’ll normalize upstream (Infra) rather than accept arbitrary strings in the validator.
